title: Consumer! Beware, Be Aware
summary: ## Who is a consumer; problems faced

A consumer is a person who buys or uses goods or services to satisfy needs. The Consumer Protection Act (CPA) 1986 recognises one who buys and uses goods and one who hires or avails a service for personal use. Problems of consumers: (1) Price variation – the Maximum Retail Price (MRP) printed on the product includes all taxes; never pay more, and take a receipt; (2) lack of standardised products – substandard goods give shopkeepers higher commission; compare brands on price, standard mark, ease of use, after-sales service, electricity use and warranty; (3) imitation – look-alike packs and names (Colgate and 'college') and fake standard marks, a punishable offence; (4) adulteration – adding inferior substances or removing a vital part to earn more profit; (5) non-availability, black-marketing and hoarding; (6) defective weights and measures; (7) misleading or no information – tiny labels, 'free' gifts, exaggerated advertisements, fake sales; (8) problems related to services – gas agencies, banks, builders, railways, post, electricity.

Adulteration tests: milk with water – a drop on a tilted plate leaves no trace, or in a tumbler for 10 minutes no ring/cream; black pepper with papaya seeds – in water pepper settles while papaya seeds float; asafoetida with resin or gum – shaken in water pure hing turns milky; tea with coloured exhausted leaves – colour on blotting paper when sprinkled with water; coriander powder with dung powder – smell on soaking in water; spices with extraneous colour – colour in water; tea or semolina with iron filings – a magnet picks them up. Precautions: read labels, check genuine standard marks, buy sealed packs from reputed shops, buy whole spices and grind at home, test samples and send doubtful ones to PFA laboratories. Defective weights: false-bottomed or dented measures, stones as weights, iron rings or magnets under the pan, missing pointer, tilted balance; for cloth – a table used for measuring, bent rod, stretched fabric.

Consumer education tells the consumer what, how much, how, where, when to buy and how to pay: buy only needed things; non-perishables in bulk, semi-perishables for a week, perishables in small amounts; survey the market and read labels; buy from licensed or co-operative shops and from those who replace faulty goods; buy when shops are less crowded; seasonal fruits and vegetables; electronics and woollens off-season; check interest on credit. Consumer aids: labels, leaflets, packages, advertisements, standardisation marks, legislation and consumer organisations. Label information: name, trade and brand name, manufacturer's name and address, ingredients, purpose, directions, warnings, date of manufacture and expiry, dosage, guarantee period, standard mark, MRP, net weight and lot or batch number (needed for complaints; check ingredients for allergies, rates and net amount, expiry).

Standard marks: ISI (electrical goods, chemicals, toys, pressure cookers, biscuits, coffee), FPO (tinned and preserved foods, juices, jams, sauces, pickles), Agmark (spices, cereals, flour, pulses, eggs, oil, butter – agricultural and livestock products), Woolmark (wool and woollen garments), Hallmark (gold ornaments), Eco-mark (environment-friendly goods); ISO 9000 is a global quality-system standard. Packages protect from damage, spoilage, breakage, adulteration and pilferage and help transport. Legislation: the Consumer Protection Act 1986 (amended 2002) covers all goods and services; consumer courts at district, state and national levels. Consumer organisations give information, work for consumer welfare, guide the government, educate consumers, protest against anti-consumer activities, test products and represent complaints in consumer courts.

Rights: safety (against harmful goods such as adulterated food or unsafe appliances); choose (variety of good products); be informed (quality, purity, potency, ingredients, price; e.g. warnings on toxic products, a shopkeeper refusing a pamphlet violates this right); represent; be heard (express in court); seek redressal (against unfair or restrictive trade practices; compensation); consumer education; basic needs (food, clothing, health care, drinking water, sanitation, shelter, education); healthy environment. 15 March is World Consumer Rights Day. Responsibilities: survey the market, insist on and keep the bill, buy standard products, read and follow instructions, buy sealed foods, avoid wastage and hoarding, join other consumers against sellers and file complaints in the proper forum.

Filing a complaint: anyone can file within 2 years of purchase; district forum for goods or services up to Rs 20 lakh, state forum for more than Rs 20 lakh and up to Rs 1 crore, national forum for more than Rs 1 crore; nominal fees; first contact the seller and keep a record, then write to the manufacturer by registered post, then send a notice giving 15 days; fill the prescribed form with facts, attach bills, state the compensation desired and a notarised affidavit; the court notice asks the opposite party to reply within 30 days; cases are to be settled within 90 days (5 months if testing is needed). Relief: removal of defects, replacement, refund, compensation and costs.

vsa: In what four ways do consumer organisations help the consumers?

They give information; test products for quality and defects; educate consumers; protest against anti-consumer activities; guide the government in framing policies; accept complaints and represent consumers in consumer courts.
April 2026

or: Write any four responsibilities of a consumer.

Survey the market before buying; insist on and keep the bill; buy standard-mark products; read and follow instructions; buy sealed foods; file a complaint in the proper forum and join other consumers against sellers; do not encourage black marketing.

vsa: What is the importance of the information given on the label of a product?

It gives the name, ingredients (allergies or animal source), manufacturer's address, directions and warnings, net weight, MRP, batch number for complaints, and the dates of manufacture and expiry, the standard mark and guarantee, so we can choose, use safely and complain if needed.
April 2025

or: Why is it important to check the standard mark, ingredients, batch number and expiry date on the label?
Standard mark shows quality, ingredients show allergens, batch number is needed to complain to the manufacturer, and expiry date tells us not to buy products near expiry.

vsa: Mr Gupta wants to file a case against a manufacturer. What two documents would he need to submit with his complaint?
The bill or receipt (proof of purchase) and the guarantee/warranty or a notarised affidavit with the prescribed form (plus the court fee).
April 2024
Adulteration is a major problem of consumers. Support this statement with any four examples.

Water is added to milk; papaya seeds to black pepper; resin or gum to asafoetida; coloured exhausted leaves to tea; dung powder to coriander powder; iron filings to tea or semolina; extraneous colour to spices.
October 2025
Which adulterants are added to asafoetida, spices, milk and black pepper and how are they tested?

Asafoetida – resin or gum; shake in water – pure hing turns milky. Spices – extraneous colour; sprinkle in water – coloured water. Milk – water; a drop on a tilted plate leaves no trace. Black pepper – papaya seeds; in water pepper settles and papaya seeds float.
April 2023
Elaborate six points of information you would check on the label of honey before buying.
Name of the product and brand; manufacturer's name and address; ingredients; net weight; MRP; dates of manufacture and expiry or best before; batch number; standard mark such as Agmark or FPO.
October 2022
How can you check whether the milk vendor is cheating you?

Check that milk is measured to the brim, the measure is emptied completely before refilling, there is no false bottom, and the measure has the inspector's stamp with date; test dilution with a tilted plate or by keeping it in a tumbler.
How can the cloth merchant cheat in measuring? Name any four signs.
Using a table to measure, a bent measuring rod, stretching the fabric while measuring, and selling cheap fabric at the price of a better one.
April 2024
sa: Write any six characteristic features of a good label of a food product.

Name of the product and brand; manufacturer's name and address; ingredients; date of manufacture and date of expiry; net weight; MRP; directions for use and storage; standard mark (Agmark, FPO, ISI); lot or batch number; guarantee or warnings.
Explain any six problems faced by a consumer and how to tackle one of them.

Price variation (charging above MRP); lack of standardised products; imitation of brands and marks; adulteration; hoarding and black marketing; defective weights and measures; misleading advertisements and sales; poor services. To tackle price variation: survey the market, never pay more than MRP and take a bill to complain.
Describe the steps of filing a complaint in a consumer court.

Contact the seller and keep a record; write to the manufacturer by registered post; send a notice to the opposite party giving 15 days; fill the prescribed form with details and facts, attach bills and court fee, specify compensation and attach a notarised affidavit; submit to the receiving clerk of the consumer court (district up to Rs 20 lakh, state up to Rs 1 crore, national above that); the court notifies the other party who must reply in 30 days; the case is to be settled in 90 days.
la: Explain any five rights of a consumer with an example of each.

(1) Right to safety – a cooker that bursts or adulterated food; complain against the manufacturer. (2) Right to choose – a shopkeeper cannot keep just one brand of toothpaste. (3) Right to be informed – a shopkeeper who refuses the product booklet can be taken to court. (4) Right to be heard – express yourself in court if cheated. (5) Right to seek redressal – compensation for faulty goods or unfair trade practices. (6) Right to consumer education – knowledge of consumer evils. (7) Right to basic needs and a healthy environment.
Write the consumer aids available to a consumer and the information a label must give (five points each).

Aids: labels, leaflets, packages, advertisements, standardisation marks (ISI, FPO, Agmark, Woolmark, Hallmark, Eco-mark), legislation (Consumer Protection Act) and consumer organisations. A label gives the name of the product, manufacturer's name and address, ingredients, directions for use, warnings, date of manufacture and expiry, net weight, MRP, batch number, guarantee period and the standard mark.
